text:
It doesn't and never will David..Che k out what our founding fathers wrote...

Thomas Jefferson and John Adams (jointly), with the most extended critical writings later coming from John Quincy Adams.

In March 1786, while serving as American diplomats (Jefferson in France, Adams in Britain), they met with Sidi Haji Abdrahaman, the Tripoli ambassador in London. In a joint letter to U.S. Secretary of Foreign Affairs John Jay dated March 28, 1786, they reported the ambassador’s explanation for Barbary piracy and hostility toward nations that had done them no injury:

“The Ambassador answered us that it was founded on the Laws of their Prophet, that it was written in their Koran, that all nations who should not have acknowledged their authority were sinners, that it was their right and duty to make war upon them wherever they could be found, and to make slaves of all they could take as Prisoners, and that every Muslim man who should be slain in battle was sure to go to Paradise.”

This documented the religious justification offered by the Barbary states for raiding shipping, taking captives, and demanding tribute—an issue the young United States faced after independence removed British naval protection. Jefferson in particular studied the Quran (he owned a copy of George Sale’s 1734 translation) and favored a naval response over continued payments.

John Quincy Adams (son of John Adams, and later the sixth U.S. president) later wrote more expansive critiques. In essays published around 1830, he described Muhammad as combining “the powers of transcendent genius, with the preternatural energy of a fanatic, and the fraudulent spirit of an impostor,” and stated that “the precept of the koran is, perpetual war against all who deny, that Mohammed is the prophet of God.” He contrasted this with Christian teachings and noted the long history of conflict.

Other Founding-era figures held varied views. Many supported religious liberty that theoretically included Muslims (Jefferson, Washington, Franklin, and others referenced “Mahometans” in arguments for tolerance). Franklin used Islamic imagery in a satirical 1790 piece on the slave trade, putting pro-slavery arguments into the mouth of a fictional Algerian official who cited the Quran’s allowance of slavery and the conquest of non-believers—highlighting hypocrisy rather than issuing a direct warning.

In short, the clearest contemporary record of Founding Fathers recording and conveying the religious rationale for aggression from Muslim powers is the 1786 Adams-Jefferson letter, while John Quincy Adams provided the most developed later analysis. Views among the Founders were not uniform and coexisted with strong commitments to religious liberty.

text:
**The era of AI-driven power demand has arrived.**

In a research note dated October 26, Morgan Stanley raised its forecast for the net power deficit at U.S. data centers for the 2026–2028 period to 38 GW, up from its previous estimate of 33 GW. Within the semiconductor sector, the firm’s top picks are Nvidia ($NVDA) and Broadcom ($AVGO), citing their conservative guidance, clear visibility on chip rollouts, and—in Nvidia’s case—superior token output per watt. The bank also noted that in an environment constrained by power availability, ASICs could potentially lose market share to GPUs, as the former offer lower token output per watt.

This may represent a major, once-in-a-generation opportunity to build significant wealth over the next decade.

Below are 8 stocks linked to the AI-power theme that hold the potential for 10x growth or more:

1. $NVDA (Nvidia) — A top semiconductor pick for Morgan Stanley, with a price target of $300—implying a 42.2% upside from its October 22 closing price of $210.96.

2. $AVGO (Broadcom) — A top semiconductor pick for Morgan Stanley, with a price target of $505—implying a 57.0% upside from its October 22 closing price of $321.88.

3. $CEG (Constellation Energy) — Rated "Overweight" by Morgan Stanley with a price target of $378; a nuclear power plant operator that leads the industry in power supply contracts for data centers.

4. $VST (Vistra) — An independent power producer that sells electricity directly to AI data centers, though it carries a higher debt-to-equity ratio than Constellation.

5. $GEV (GE Vernova) — A "shovel seller" for the AI-power infrastructure build-out; the company boasts a massive order backlog, with an increasing share of its gas-power equipment destined for data center clients.

6. $OKLO (Oklo) — A play on small modular reactors (SMRs); investors are closely watching the progress of its project in Groves, Texas, from the initial groundbreaking to achieving first criticality. 7. $SMR (NuScale Power) — A representative of the small modular reactor (SMR) pathway. Commercialization milestones have lagged behind expectations; keep an eye on progress regarding final power purchase agreements (PPAs).

8. $ETR (Entergy) — A regulated utility in the U.S. South, serving regions with a high concentration of data centers (such as Louisiana). It exhibits lower volatility compared to independent power producers.

Take note. Completely free of charge.

**Risk Warning:** The "AI-driven power demand" narrative is highly polarized. A Morgan Stanley research report notes that if infrastructure development stalls, the greatest disruption will likely occur at the end of the "bullwhip effect"—impacting downstream components like energy storage and optical modules, as well as power management and analog devices that may have been over-ordered during a potential market downturn. While the story of rising power demand is a decade-long trend, stock prices could potentially price in five years' worth of expectations within just three months.

Kartik Maas Deep Daan  begins today, 27 October 2026, according to the North Indian Purnimanta tradition, and continue every evening until Kartik Purnima, 24 November 2026. Some Vaishnava traditions began their lamp offerings on 26 October.

Kartik Deep Daan Vidhi

* After sunset, light a clay diya with pure ghee or sesame oil.

* Offer one diya near Tulsi Mata and another at your home entrance.

* You may also offer a diya at a Vishnu or Shiva temple.

* Chant ॐ नमो भगवते वासुदेवाय 11 times.

* Pray for inner purification, wisdom, family harmony and divine grace.

Deeper spiritual significance: In Kartik Maas, Deep Daan symbolises the removal of ignorance and the awakening of divine consciousness. The Padma Purana particularly praises offering lamps during this sacred month.

Even one diya offered daily with sincere devotion is meaningful. There is no need for elaborate arrangements.

Important: Kartik Deep Daan is traditionally performed in the evening, preferably after sunset. Keep the diya in a safe location.

text:
Lessons 1-3 from the Divine Office for the Fourth Sunday of October: II Machabees 1:1-22
.
To the brethren the Jews that are throughout Egypt, the brethren, the Jews that are in Jerusalem, and in the land of Judea, send health, and good peace.  May God be gracious to you, and remember His covenant that He made with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, His faithful servants: And give you all a heart to worship Him, and to do His will with a great heart, and a willing mind. May He open your heart in His law, and in His commandments, and send you peace.  May He hear your prayers, and be reconciled unto you, and never forsake you in the evil time. And now here we are praying for you.  When Demetrius reigned, in the year one hundred and sixty-nine, we Jews wrote to you, in the trouble, and violence, that came upon us in those years, after Jason withdrew himself from the holy land, and from the kingdom.  They burnt the gate, and shed innocent blood: then we prayed to the Lord, and were heard, and we offered sacrifices, and fine flour, and lighted the lamps, and set forth the loaves.  And now celebrate ye the days of Scenopegia in the month of Casleu.  In the year one hundred and eighty-eight, the people that is at Jerusalem, and in Judea, and the senate, and Judas, to Aristobolus, the preceptor of king Ptolemee, who is of the stock of the anointed priests, and to the Jews that are in Egypt, health and welfare.  Having been delivered by God out of great dangers, we give Him great thanks, forasmuch as we have been in war with such a king. ] For he made numbers of men swarm out of Persia that have fought against us, and the holy city.  For when the leader himself was in Persia, and with him a very great army, he fell in the temple of Nanea, being deceived by the counsel of the priests of Nanea.  For Antiochus, with his friends, came to the place as though he would marry her, and that he might receive great sums of money under the title of a dowry.  And when the priests of Nanea had set it forth, and he with a small company had entered into the compass of the temple, they shut the temple, When Antiochus was come in: and opening a secret entrance of the temple, they cast stones and slew the leader, and them that were with him, and hewed them in pieces, and cutting off their heads they threw them forth.  Blessed be God in all things, Who hath delivered up the wicked. Therefore whereas we purpose to keep the purification of the temple on the five and twentieth day of the month of Casleu, we thought it necessary to signify it to you: that you also may keep the day of Scenopegia, and the day of the fire, that was given when Nehemias offered sacrifice, after the temple and the altar was built.  For when our fathers were led into Persia, the priests that then were worshippers of God took privately the fire from the altar, and hid it in a valley where there was a deep pit without water, and there they kept it safe, so that the place was unknown to all men.  But when many years had passed, and it pleased God that Nehemias should be sent by the king of Persia, he sent some of the posterity of those priests that had hid it, to seek for the fire: and as they told us, they found no fire, but thick water. Then he bade them draw it up, and bring it to him: and the priest Nehemias commanded the sacrifices that were laid on, to be sprinkled with the same water, both the wood, and the things that were laid upon it.  And when this was done, and the time came that the sun shone out, which before was in a cloud, there was a great fire kindled, so that all wondered.

text:
$SPCX

Musk Says 2–3 Years. The Real Battle Starts With Spectrum.
STARLINK MOBILE AND THE FCC
Why SpaceX Is Targeting NextNav's 902–928 MHz Spectrum
CHECK & COMMENT
SpaceX ($SPCX) has taken another step toward entering the U.S. wireless market.
This time, it's not about rockets or satellites.
SpaceX has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to expand the spectrum bands eligible for satellite-to-phone connectivity, commonly known as Direct-to-Device (D2D).

I see this development as a continuation of the recent debate between Verizon's CEO and Elon Musk over how quickly SpaceX can build a competitive wireless network.

Competing with America's established mobile carriers requires more than launching satellites. It also requires spectrum access, terrestrial infrastructure, and regulatory approval.

1. What exactly did SpaceX request?

On October 21–22, SpaceX representatives met with FCC officials to discuss expanding the regulatory framework for Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS).

One particular frequency range stands out: 902–928 MHz.

SpaceX asked the FCC to consider including this band in its expanded SCS rules.

The company specifically referenced NextNav ($NN), which has been pursuing a proposal to establish nationwide 5G spectrum rights in this frequency range.

SpaceX's reasoning is relatively straightforward.

If the FCC eventually approves NextNav's proposed spectrum restructuring, establishing an SCS framework for this band in advance could reduce the need for additional rulemaking procedures.

There is one important distinction.

This request does not mean SpaceX has secured the spectrum or entered into a commercial agreement with NextNav.

2. What is NextNav?

NextNav is a U.S. technology company developing terrestrial positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) systems that can complement or provide backup capabilities to GPS.

In 2024, NextNav petitioned the FCC to modify the rules governing the 902–928 MHz band to support a terrestrial 5G-based PNT network.

Its core business objective is to provide reliable positioning and timing services, including when GPS signals are disrupted or unavailable.

This is where the potential interests of NextNav and SpaceX intersect.

NextNav wants regulatory approval for its terrestrial 5G and PNT infrastructure.

SpaceX wants the regulatory flexibility to potentially use relevant spectrum for satellite-to-phone services in the future.

However, there has been no confirmed announcement of a spectrum lease, joint venture, or commercial partnership between the two companies.

NextNav's recent stock-price reaction should therefore be distinguished from the value of any actual signed agreement.

3. Why does 902–928 MHz matter?

Spectrum is one of the most valuable assets in the wireless industry.

Lower-frequency bands generally offer advantages in geographic coverage and indoor signal penetration.

For SpaceX, which is exploring a combination of satellite connectivity and terrestrial wireless infrastructure, access to additional spectrum could create new business opportunities.

But there is another side to this issue.

The 902–928 MHz band is already used by numerous industrial and unlicensed wireless devices.

Utilities, smart meters, security systems, industrial equipment, and other existing users have legitimate interests in how this spectrum is managed.

Any new service must address potential harmful interference with existing operations.

A frequency band being technically attractive does not automatically mean it is commercially available.

Regulatory authorization and interference protection remain essential.

4. Why October 29 matters

On Thursday, October 29, the FCC is scheduled to consider a proposal to modernize and expand its SCS rules.

The draft proposal would broaden the spectrum available for satellite-to-device services, including consideration of approximately 482 MHz of additional spectrum.

SpaceX wants the FCC to include the NextNav-related 902–928 MHz band in that regulatory discussion.

However, even if the FCC adopts the proposal, it would represent a step in the rulemaking process, not final authorization for commercial operations.

NextNav's underlying spectrum restructuring petition would also remain a separate regulatory matter.

I will be watching three developments closely:

Whether 902–928 MHz is included in the FCC's proposed SCS framework.

How the FCC proceeds with NextNav's separate spectrum petition.

Whether SpaceX eventually discloses a concrete spectrum agreement or deployment plan.

5. Connecting this to Musk's 2–3 year timeline
Recently, Verizon's CEO argued that SpaceX would need at least four to six years, along with substantial capital investment, to build a competitive nationwide wireless network.
Elon Musk responded that it would take just two to three years.

I believe this FCC filing adds an important piece to that debate.

SpaceX is already operating satellite-to-phone services while preparing to expand its next-generation Starlink Mobile V2 satellite constellation and terrestrial infrastructure.

Now it is also seeking greater regulatory flexibility over spectrum access.

That does not prove Musk's timeline is achievable.

Competing with established mobile carriers requires sufficient network capacity, reliable service quality, customer acquisition, and a viable return on infrastructure investment.

Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile also possess substantial competitive advantages.

Nevertheless, SpaceX appears to be addressing several of the necessary building blocks simultaneously: satellites, spectrum, ground infrastructure, and regulation.

6. What this means for our SpaceX investment thesis

I view this development as another indication of Starlink Mobile's potential expansion into a much larger market.

Our long-term SpaceX investment thesis has focused on several interconnected capabilities:

Reusable rockets and independent access to space.

Starlink's global communications network.

Expanding AI computing infrastructure.

Starshield and national security communications.

Now, the possibility of directly competing in the U.S. terrestrial wireless market adds another dimension.

That could eventually create a substantial new revenue opportunity.

However, it could also require significant investment in spectrum, cellular infrastructure, regulatory compliance, and customer acquisition.

We should not value this opportunity based solely on the size of the addressable market.

What matters is whether SpaceX can convert this expansion into sustainable revenue, attractive returns on invested capital, and free cash flow.

7. My final assessment

I see SpaceX's latest FCC request as a constructive step in preparing for a broader wireless strategy.

But I would not interpret it as confirmation that SpaceX has obtained NextNav's spectrum or that the two companies have established a commercial partnership.

What matters is that SpaceX is working on multiple elements required to expand its wireless business.

Musk has suggested a two-to-three-year timeline.

We can now begin evaluating that timeline against actual developments rather than relying solely on his confidence.

The question I care about is not how quickly Musk says SpaceX can build the future, but how much spectrum, infrastructure, and operational capability the company can actually secure.

And ultimately, I want to see whether these investments translate into sustainable cash flow and long-term shareholder value.

That remains the standard by which I evaluate SpaceX.

text:
$SPCX 
머스크의 2~3년, 진짜 승부는 주파수에서 시작된다
STARLINK MOBILE AND THE FCC
SpaceX가 NextNav의 902~928MHz에 주목한 이유

**SpaceX($SPCX)가 미국 이동통신 시장 진출을 위해 또 하나의 움직임을 보였습니다.**

이번에는 로켓도 위성도 아닙니다.

미국 연방통신위원회(FCC)에 위성 직접연결(D2D) 서비스에 활용할 수 있는 주파수 범위를 확대해 달라고 요청했습니다.

저는 이번 소식을 앞서 Verizon CEO와 일론 머스크가 벌인 통신망 구축 논쟁의 연장선에서 바라보고 있습니다.

**미국의 기존 이동통신사와 경쟁하려면 위성 발사 능력뿐 아니라 주파수와 지상망, 규제 승인이 모두 필요하기 때문입니다.**

1. SpaceX는 무엇을 요청했나?

10월 21~22일 SpaceX 관계자들은 FCC 관계자들을 만나 위성 보완통신(SCS) 관련 규칙의 개선을 제안했습니다.

그중 주목할 부분은 902~928MHz 대역입니다.

SpaceX는 FCC가 위성-휴대전화 직접연결 서비스에 활용할 수 있는 주파수 범위를 확대할 때 이 대역도 검토 대상에 포함해 달라고 요청했습니다.

특히 NextNav($NN)가 추진하고 있는 전국적인 5G 주파수 이용권 제안을 언급했습니다.

SpaceX의 논리는 비교적 명확합니다.

FCC가 향후 NextNav의 주파수 재편 제안을 승인할 경우, 해당 대역의 위성 직접연결 활용을 위한 별도 규칙 제정 절차를 줄일 수 있도록 미리 준비하자는 것입니다.

중요한 점이 있습니다.

**이번 요청은 주파수 사용 승인이나 NextNav와의 계약 체결을 의미하지 않습니다.**

2. NextNav는 어떤 기업인가?

NextNav는 GPS를 보완할 수 있는 지상 기반 위치·항법·시각 동기화(PNT) 기술을 개발하는 미국 기업입니다.

2024년 FCC에 902~928MHz 대역의 이용 규칙을 변경해 5G 기반 PNT 서비스를 구축할 수 있도록 요청했습니다.

NextNav가 추진하는 핵심 사업은 GPS 장애가 발생했을 때도 위치와 시간 정보를 제공할 수 있는 지상 기반 보완망입니다.

여기에서 SpaceX와 NextNav 사이에 잠재적인 이해관계가 형성됩니다.

NextNav는 지상 기반 5G·PNT 서비스를 구축하려 하고, SpaceX는 향후 해당 주파수 자산이 위성 직접연결에도 활용될 수 있는 규제환경을 원하고 있습니다.

하지만 현재 양사 간 주파수 임대계약이나 공동사업 계약이 체결됐다는 공식 발표는 확인되지 않았습니다.

NextNav의 주가 상승 역시 미래 사업 가능성에 대한 시장의 기대와 실제 계약 가치를 구분해서 봐야 합니다.

3. 왜 902~928MHz가 중요한가?

주파수는 이동통신 사업에서 매우 중요한 자산입니다.

특히 상대적으로 낮은 주파수 대역은 넓은 지역을 커버하고 건물 내부에 신호를 전달하는 데 유리한 특성이 있습니다.

SpaceX가 위성망과 지상망을 결합하려 한다면 이러한 주파수 자산은 새로운 사업 기회가 될 수 있습니다.

그러나 해당 대역은 현재 다양한 산업용·비면허 통신기기에서 활용되고 있습니다.

전력회사와 산업시설의 통신장비, 스마트 계량기, 보안장치 등 기존 이용자들의 이해관계도 얽혀 있습니다.

따라서 새로운 서비스 도입으로 기존 장비에 유해한 간섭이 발생하지 않는지 검증해야 합니다.

**주파수가 기술적으로 매력적이라는 것과 상업적으로 사용할 수 있다는 것은 다른 문제입니다.**

4. 10월 29일 FCC 회의가 중요합니다.

이번 주 목요일인 10월 29일 FCC는 위성 직접연결 서비스 관련 규칙을 확대하는 제안을 검토할 예정입니다.

현재 초안에는 SCS 활용 대상 주파수를 확대하고, 추가로 약 482MHz를 검토하는 내용이 포함돼 있습니다.

SpaceX는 이번 논의에 NextNav 관련 902~928MHz 대역도 포함해 달라고 요청했습니다.

그러나 회의에서 제안이 채택되더라도 이는 후속 의견수렴을 위한 규칙 제정 절차의 시작입니다.

실제 주파수 사용 승인과는 구분해야 합니다.

또한 NextNav의 주파수 재편 청원 자체가 이번 회의에서 최종 승인되는 것도 아닙니다.

저는 다음 세 가지를 확인하려고 합니다.

902~928MHz가 실제 규칙 제정 검토 대상에 포함되는가?

NextNav의 별도 주파수 재편 절차는 어떻게 진행되는가?

SpaceX가 향후 구체적인 사용계약이나 서비스 계획을 발표하는가?

5. 머스크가 말한 2~3년과 연결하면

최근 Verizon CEO는 SpaceX가 경쟁력 있는 미국 이동통신망을 구축하려면 최소 4~6년과 막대한 자본이 필요하다고 주장했습니다.

머스크는 2~3년이면 가능하다고 반박했습니다.

저는 이번 FCC 요청이 그 논쟁의 중요한 후속 움직임이라고 생각합니다.

SpaceX는 이미 위성 직접연결 서비스를 운영하고 있으며, 차세대 Mobile V2 위성과 지상 통신 인프라 확대도 추진하고 있습니다.

여기에 주파수 활용 범위까지 확대하려는 것입니다.

다만 이러한 움직임만으로 머스크의 시간표가 실현 가능하다고 판단할 수는 없습니다.

실제 이동통신 시장에서 경쟁하려면 충분한 네트워크 용량과 서비스 품질, 고객 확보, 그리고 투자비 회수가 필요합니다.

기존 통신사들의 경쟁력도 여전히 강력합니다.

6. 우리의 SpaceX 투자 논리

저는 이번 사건을 Starlink Mobile의 사업 확장 가능성을 보여주는 또 하나의 신호로 평가합니다.

우리는 그동안 SpaceX의 경쟁력을 재사용 로켓, 글로벌 위성통신망, AI 컴퓨팅, 국가안보 인프라에서 찾아왔습니다.

그런데 이제 미국의 기존 이동통신 시장에 직접 진출하려는 움직임까지 확인되고 있습니다.

이는 새로운 매출 기회가 될 수 있습니다.

하지만 동시에 주파수 확보 비용, 지상망 구축비용, 경쟁사 대응, 규제 승인이라는 새로운 부담도 발생할 수 있습니다.

따라서 시장 규모만으로 투자 가치를 판단해서는 안 됩니다.

**실제 서비스가 얼마나 많은 고객을 확보하고, 투자한 자본을 얼마나 효율적으로 회수할 수 있는지가 중요합니다.**

7. 최종 판단

저는 이번 SpaceX의 FCC 요청을 긍정적인 사업 준비 과정으로 보고 있습니다.

하지만 NextNav의 주파수를 이미 확보했다거나 양사의 협력이 확정됐다고 해석하지는 않겠습니다.

중요한 것은 SpaceX가 이동통신 사업 확대를 위해 위성, 지상망, 주파수, 규제라는 여러 요소를 동시에 준비하고 있다는 점입니다.

앞서 머스크는 2~3년을 이야기했습니다.

이제 우리는 그 시간표가 실제 사업 실행으로 뒷받침되는지를 확인할 수 있는 단계에 들어서고 있습니다.

**제가 앞으로 주목할 것은 머스크가 얼마나 빠른 미래를 이야기하느냐보다, 그 미래를 실현하기 위한 주파수와 통신 인프라를 실제로 얼마나 확보하느냐입니다.**

그리고 궁극적으로는 이 모든 투자가 SpaceX의 지속적인 현금흐름과 주주가치로 연결되는지를 확인하겠습니다.

text:
Ben Johnson was earning just $30 a month as a cowboy on an Oklahoma ranch when an unexpected opportunity changed his life. In 1940, at age 22, he agreed to deliver a dozen horses to Arizona for $300—ten months of wages for a single trip. Hollywood producer Howard Hughes noticed his extraordinary ability with horses and offered him a job as a wrangler. For seven years, Johnson worked behind the scenes, handling horses and performing dangerous stunts for stars like John Wayne, Gary Cooper, and James Stewart. Everything changed in 1948 when Johnson chased down a runaway wagon carrying three men during the filming of Fort Apache. Director John Ford witnessed the incredible feat and offered him a contract worth $5,000 a week. Johnson transitioned from stuntman to actor, appearing in Western classics such as She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, Rio Grande, and Wagon Master.
But Hollywood fame wasn't his greatest ambition. Raised by a father who was a world-champion roper, Johnson felt a deep calling to the rodeo arena. In 1953, he walked away from acting for an entire year to pursue that dream. He competed in major rodeos across the country and ultimately became the World Champion Team Roper. The victory came at a price: after a year of travel and competition expenses, he had virtually no money left. Yet he had achieved something deeply personal. Johnson eventually returned to Hollywood, continuing to compete in rodeos and using his success to support charitable events. In 1971, he accepted a role in The Last Picture Show after John Ford persuaded him to reconsider the script. His portrayal of Sam the Lion earned widespread acclaim, and in 1972, he won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. During his acceptance speech, he declared that his rodeo championship belt meant more to him than the Oscar, earning a standing ovation.
Johnson continued acting for decades, appearing in more than 300 productions while remaining devoted to his ranching and rodeo roots. He helped organize celebrity rodeos that raised millions for children's hospitals and received numerous honors, including induction into the ProRodeo Hall of Fame and a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. He died of a heart attack in 1996 at the age of 77, leaving behind an extraordinary legacy. Ben Johnson achieved what few people could even imagine: he became both an Academy Award-winning actor and a world rodeo champion, bridging two vastly different worlds without abandoning either. He may have called himself a cowboy who got lucky, but luck alone doesn't tame runaway horses, win world championships, or deliver an Oscar-winning performance. His life was proof that success means little if you lose touch with who you are—and that the greatest achievement is reaching the top without forgetting where you started.

Surpassing Defense: Debt servicing costs have officially surpassed total federal spending on national defense ($956 billion).

Revenue Consumption: Net interest payments swallow up roughly 19% of all federal revenuecollected by the government. [1, 2]

If you are interested in looking at how changing interest rates or future debt accumulations impact fiscal projections, let me know.

text:
A Jamaican woman of about fifty lay face down in the dirt outside Sevastopol while soldiers shouted at her to stay down. It was the eighteenth of June 1855, and Mary Seacole had walked seven miles in the dark the night before to work out where the assault was coming, then packed two mules with sandwiches and bandages and ridden out at first light. She dislocated her thumb throwing herself clear of a shell that morning and washed her hands in sherry because there was no water, and that thumb never went back into shape. Understand that nobody sent her and nobody paid her, and every time they ordered her off that field the bag of bandages got her back on.

Sixteen months later she was standing in a London courtroom, and the petition that had put her there was filed on the twenty-seventh of October, 1856. It named two people, and it is the reason we know exactly what the British state thought she was.

Mary Seacole, and Thomas Day the younger, of number one Tavistock Street in Covent Garden, and lately of Spring Hill and Balaklava, in the Crimea.

Then it said what they had been. Provision merchants, traders, dealers and chapmen.

Chapman is an old English word for a peddler. It is the word the state reached for when it had to write down what a woman had been doing for the British Army for thirteen months on the wrong side of the Black Sea.

Not nurse, not doctress, peddler.

Seacole was past fifty and she had come home broke. The first hearing was set for the seventh of November, at the Bankruptcy Court in Basinghall Street.

She came in person, which she did not have to do.

The Times sent a man. He wrote that the lady of colour in the room had been honoured with four government medals for her kindness to the British soldiery, that she had them pinned to her chest, and that the colours of them sat nicely with the rest of her dress.

He wrote it the way you write up a curiosity. Nobody since has found the paperwork for those medals.

There is no notice in the London Gazette, no citation, no ceremony, and no record anywhere of somebody handing them over. The campaign medals of that war went to officers and to enlisted men, which she was not and could never have been.

Her biographers think she most likely bought them herself, the small dress copies that anybody could pick up in a shop. She never once claimed them in her book.

She just wore them.

So read that court report again. A woman walked into the room where they were about to declare her insolvent wearing the recognition her country had never issued her, because she had decided she had earned it.

The British Army had already put its own account of her in writing, months before that hearing.

She carried that paper home in her luggage to a court that wrote her down as a peddler, and she died without her country ever putting a better word on her in any document it kept.

The training behind that sentence started in a boarding house in Kingston. Her mother ran it, a free Jamaican woman and a doctress, which in the Caribbean of that century meant a trained practitioner of Creole medicine.

She wrote later that she practised first on her doll, then on the dogs and cats, and finally on herself. She was twelve when she started nursing beside her mother in earnest.

After that she learned the way people learn when nobody is teaching them.

Kingston burned in 1843 and took her house with it, and she rebuilt it and restocked it. Cholera came through the island in 1850, took a washerwoman everybody knew, and she watched it work and made notes.

Then she went to Panama, and the notes turned into something else. Her brother had a store and hotel at Cruces, on the mule road that carried the California gold crowds from one ocean to the other.

She followed him there with crates of preserves and a medicine chest, and cholera arrived a few weeks behind her. There was no doctor in Cruces.

One night the biggest mule-owner in the town came and begged her to walk out to his kraal, where his men were dying. It was raining hard and the fields were flooded, and he brought a pair of tall boots for her to wade in.

She found the whole household in one long hut.

The sick and the well together, the women, the mules stabled under the same roof with their forefeet locked, and the saddles and harness heaped up beside them. The air in there nearly turned her round at the door.

She stayed. She had the doors and shutters thrown open and fires lit, worked through the night with the bravest of the women helping her, and put up rough screens around the two men she already knew she was going to lose.

Some time after midnight she sat down in front of the fire with the last of her patients in her lap. A brown-faced orphan baby, not yet a year old, and nothing left in the chest that would do it any good.

She wrote afterwards that she thought more about that child than about the men fighting for their lives behind the screens, and that she prayed over it. Towards morning it died in her arms.

Then she did the thing almost nobody knows about her.

At cold grey dawn she followed the man who was carrying the body away to bury it. She paid him to take it down an unfrequented path to the river instead, to cross with her, and to stand with her in the bush on the far bank while she found out what the disease had actually done inside a body.

She had no medical school behind her and no permission from anybody. She had a bribed gravedigger, a substitute for a scalpel, and a dead child she had already wept over.

They buried the baby under a piece of turf and walked back into Cruces. She said they crept in like guilty things.

She never wrote down what she found. She only said the knowledge was valuable, that she put it straight to use, and that everything she did in the Crimea four years later came out of that morning on the riverbank.

Cruces thanked her for it on the fourth of July, when the American storekeepers held their independence dinner at her brother's hotel and toasted her, because she had pulled a fair number of them through the cholera. The man who stood up said God bless her, she was the best yellow woman He ever made.

There were only two things the room regretted, he said. One was that she was not a citizen of the United States, and the other was her colour, and if they could have bleached her they would have.

She stood up and told them she would decline the bleaching. She said that if her skin had been darker still she would have been just as useful and just as respected by the people whose respect she valued, and that judging by the specimens of society she had met, she was not losing much by being kept out of it.

London would put the same proposition to her in politer English, and it began in the autumn of 1854, when she was in her late forties and the papers were full of what was happening to the army outside Sevastopol. She knew those regiments, because the men dying of cholera out there were men she had nursed at Kingston, and some of the officers had eaten at her table.

So she went and asked to be sent.

She went to the War Office. She went to the Quartermaster General's department, and to the medical department, and to the office of the Secretary at War, carrying references from army surgeons who had watched her work.

She got nothing at any of them.

Then she found the home address of Sidney Herbert, whose wife Elizabeth was interviewing the women going out as nurses. She went to the house in Belgrave Square and waited in the great hall.

She waited a long time, and scores of people passed her going in and coming out. She wrote afterwards that the footmen marvelled at the yellow woman that no excuse could get rid of and no rudeness could put off.

Eventually one of the nursing party came out to her and said the complement was full. Then came the coldest sentence in her book.

She read in the woman's face that if there had been a vacancy, she would not have been the one to fill it.

She had one thing left to try. There was a fund collecting money to send help out to the army, and she asked them to pay her passage, and they refused as well.

Then she walked out into the street and stood there and cried. She wrote down the question she asked herself standing there, which was whether American prejudice against colour had put down roots in England too, and whether those ladies were shrinking from her aid because her blood ran under a duskier skin than theirs.

The record here is more tangled than the version that goes round, and the truth of it is not kinder.

The famous first party of nurses had already sailed by the time she started knocking, and the second party was gone by early December. She was late, she never filed the formal written application with references, and she never went to the address in Queen's Square where women without hospital experience were meant to be assessed.

Florence Nightingale was in Turkey through all of it and had no part in any of those refusals. The two of them met once, months later at Scutari, and by Seacole's own account it was short and perfectly civil and Nightingale had a bed found for her for the night.

So the record does not show a duel between two women. It shows a country with five or six doors, all of which a woman in her late forties with thirty years of practice behind her was permitted to stand outside.

She stopped asking.

A relative of her late husband named Thomas Day was going out to Balaclava on business, and the two of them put their money together and formed a firm. Seacole and Day, provision merchants.

The camp wits renamed it the moment they heard it. Day and Martin, they called it, after the London boot-blacking company, because of the colour of the pair of them.

She wrote the joke into her own book.

She had cards printed and sent on ahead, announcing that Mrs Seacole, late of Jamaica, would be opening a mess table and comfortable quarters for sick and convalescent officers near Balaclava. She sailed at the end of January 1855 on a Dutch steamer called the Hollander and reached Balaclava on the nineteenth of March aboard a cattle transport.

She was about fifty, and she was paying for all of it herself.

On the twenty-third of March, Thomas Day wrote to Major General Richard Airey asking leave to put up three iron houses on unoccupied ground. That letter sat unindexed in a box at the National Archives at Kew until a researcher pulled it out by accident.

They got the ground two miles out from Balaclava, and she named it Spring Hill. They built the British Hotel out of salvage, driftwood and packing cases and sheets of iron, with glass doors and window frames carried off from the emptied village of Kamara.

It was never a hospital and she never said it was. It was a store, a kitchen, a bar and a canteen, it sold to officers at officers' prices, and it made money.

While the huts were still going up, she started walking down to the wharf at Balaclava.

That was where the sick lay waiting for the ships that would carry them to the hospitals across the water at Scutari. Some days more than two hundred men went out on one tide.

She brought a stove and a kettle and stood there brewing tea for whoever wanted it, in rain and snow, day after day, at a post nobody had assigned her. An assistant surgeon who watched her do it wrote it down years later, and Russell of the Times wrote it into a dispatch.

She brought lemonade and sponge cake as well. In her own account of it there is a phrase that tells you the whole shape of her position out there.

She gave the men, she wrote, all the doctors would allow her to give.

There was a ceiling on what a woman like her was permitted to hand a wounded British soldier, and the ceiling was tea, lemonade and cake.

She went round that ceiling three times, and the first was the eighteenth of June, 1855.

On the Sunday evening before, something in the camp gossip at Spring Hill got into her. She could not sit still, and instead of going to bed she wrapped up against the cold and walked the three and a half miles to Cathcart's Hill.

She stayed up there past midnight. In the dark she worked out what was happening, because regiment after regiment was moving quietly down towards the trenches, and that meant the assault would come at dawn.

She walked home and did not sleep.

The rest of that short night the whole house was up cutting bread and cheese and making sandwiches, packing fowls and tongues and ham, wine and spirits. She filled the big bag she always carried slung across her shoulder with lint, bandages, needles, thread and medicines.

Everything went onto two mules with her steadiest lad in charge. She led out on horseback, and the little cavalcade left the British Hotel before the sun of the eighteenth of June was many hours old.

The cavalry pickets stopped her, because their orders were to keep stragglers and sightseers away from the fighting. Then they worked out who she was and what was on the mules, and the men gave her a shout, and their officer waved her through.

She left the mules at Cathcart's Hill and loaded herself with as much as she could carry.

She got through to the reserves of Sir Henry Barnard's division, and the officers there relieved her of the food while the wounded took what was in the bag. Then she worked her way to the temporary hospital on the Woronzoff Road, where the surgeons were going flat out, and she started binding wounds.

She was under fire on the way and under fire when she got there. Shot came ploughing up the ground and shell went over, and the men around her would shout, lie down, mother, lie down.

So she would throw herself flat in the dirt and stay there until somebody laughed and told her the old lady could get up again.

She was ordered back more than once that day. Each time, she wrote, the bag of bandages was her passport.

One of those times she went down too fast to get clear of a shell and landed hard on her right hand, and dislocated the thumb. Somebody bound it on the spot.

It never went back to its proper shape, and she carried the crooked thumb for the rest of her life.

There was no water to wash in, so she rinsed her hands in sherry and carried on. When she got back to Cathcart's Hill her horse was there and the boy was not, having lost his nerve and gone off with both mules, so she rode three miles to catch him.

Then she turned round and worked her way to the far left, where General Eyre's division had been cut up all day, left her horse with some men, and crept down to where the wounded were lying to leave them what she had.

She got back to Spring Hill after dark. Everyone there had watched the battle from safe ground and could tell her exactly how the day had gone, and she noted that she, who had been in the middle of it since dawn, knew almost nothing about it.

The assault on the Redan had failed. Two of the men who died in front of it had been sitting in her place a few days before.

Colonel Lacy Yea had been teasing her that she needed a silver salver to hand things round on, instead of the shabby one she had been reduced to. Sir John Campbell had been her patron for years, and his wife had once lodged in her house in Kingston.

She had delivered their baby there. A little Scotchman, she called him, born within sight of the blue hills of Jamaica and put into his father's arms by her.

The next day there was an armistice, and she went out onto the ground to look at the faces of the men who had been kind to her.

It was late in the afternoon before the Russians brought the two bodies across. They had stripped Campbell of his epaulettes, his sword and his boots.

She wrote one line about standing there, and it is not about herself. She thought about the people at home who did not know yet.

The second time came two months later, on the sixteenth of August, when the Russians crossed the Tchernaya. She rode out loaded up as usual and watched most of the morning from a hill.

She could see what the Russians could not, the English and French cavalry drawn up below her waiting for a chance that never came. Then the Russians fell back and she went down into the field with everybody else.

She dressed French and Sardinian wounds and helped lift men into the ambulances. She also treated Russians, and made a point of saying they were handled as kindly as the rest.

One of them was shot through the lower jaw and was past any help she had. She put a finger into his mouth to find where the ball had gone, and as he died his teeth closed on it and would not release.

She had to call the men around her to get her hand free, and she was bitten so deeply that she wrote she would carry the scar to her grave.

She did not hold it against him. As he went, she said, his rough face softened and he smiled, and then he was gone.

Another Russian, an officer shot in the side, bore it so well that she called it noble. He pulled a ring off his own finger and gave it to her, and when she had helped lift him into the ambulance he kissed her hand.

The French were stripping the dead all around her while she worked, and when she said something about it the officers laughed at her.

She took two things off that field. One was a wounded French officer who preferred to be carried back to Spring Hill and nursed there.

The other was a Cossack colt, running circles round its dam, which was lying dead beside its dead owner.

The colt had been hit in the ears and one forefoot, and a French corporal was about to put it out of its misery when she reached them. She offered him ten shillings to carry it down to the British Hotel instead.

He brought it in that evening. She dressed its wounds and reared it, and it became the pet of Spring Hill, and when she finally went home to England the colt went with her.

She would not loot. She said plainly that she could not bear the idea of plundering the living or the dead, and all she took off that field was a small metal cross and a few buttons cut from the coarse grey coats of the men lying there.

The third time was September, when Sevastopol fell and she went in with a pass, among the first British women through, and got herself arrested as a spy for her trouble.

Russell wrote her up in the Times that month as a physician who doctored and cured all manner of men with extraordinary success. That was the high-water mark of her public standing, and it lasted less than a year.

The war ended on the thirtieth of March 1856, faster than anybody at Spring Hill had planned for.

She had just laid in a great deal of stock. The army left and the customers left, and she was standing in the Crimea with shelves full of goods nobody on earth wanted and that could not be shipped home.

They pulled the iron house down and packed it up. The Russians got the outbuildings, the sheds, the kitchen fittings and the stoves that had cost so much.

About the stoves she wrote only that she hoped a cook worthy of them had them now.

She came home in August. A canteen scheme at Aldershot failed for want of money, the Crimean creditors caught up with her, and by the end of October the petition was filed.

Thomas Day wrote to the papers explaining that the collapse had been caused by the weather, by robbery, and by the sudden evacuation. She was discharged from bankruptcy on the thirtieth of January 1857.

And that is when Britain decided to be generous.

Officers who had eaten her dinners started writing to the Times. Punch, which had already drawn her as a canteen woman, ran a cartoon that December and a plea for subscriptions the following May.

Lord Rokeby, who had commanded the First Division in the Crimea, wrote to the paper in November 1856 asking the public to give.

Look closely at what he asked them to give for. The money was to enable her, in his words, to recommence the business to which she was accustomed.

Not to pay her for the wounded on the Woronzoff Road. To set her up in a shop.

Even the men who loved her could only think of one category to put her in, and it was the same one the bankruptcy court had used. Nobody was raising money to pay a nurse.

Then they threw her a party.

The Seacole Fund Grand Military Festival ran for four nights, from Monday the twenty-seventh of July to Thursday the thirtieth of July 1857, at the Royal Surrey Gardens in Kennington. The patrons' list carried the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh and the Duke of Cambridge.

The hall was the largest venue in London, cast iron, three floors, twelve thousand seats, hung for the occasion with English, French, Sardinian and Turkish flags.

Eleven military bands played. The massed musicians came from the Life Guards, the Horse Guards, the Grenadiers, the Coldstreams, the Scots Fusiliers, the Royal Engineers and the Royal Artillery, Louis Jullien conducted, and more than a thousand performers took part.

She sat up in front of the centre gallery with Lord Rokeby on one side of her and Lord George Paget on the other while the crowd stood and roared at her.

The Times reported that the gardens had never held a greater multitude, that the music hall was crammed, and that hundreds who had paid could not get through the doors. Across the four nights something like forty thousand people came.

The Royal Surrey Gardens Company had been in trouble for months and the production costs had been enormous. It went insolvent almost the moment the last band packed up.

Her share of the profits was a quarter. Fifty-seven pounds.

Four nights, eleven bands, a thousand performers, forty thousand people, three royal patrons, and fifty-seven pounds.

She published the book that same July, from lodgings at fourteen Soho Square. It was the only thing left that could actually pay her.

Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands, printed by James Blackwood, with a preface by William Howard Russell of the Times, who had watched her work in the Crimea. Russell wrote that she was the first person to redeem the word sutler from the suspicion of worthlessness and plunder.

He said he trusted England would not forget the woman who had nursed her sick.

The book sold well. It was the first autobiography published in Britain by a Black woman, written at fifty-one to climb out of a hole the war had put her in.

Thirteen years later, in August 1870, Florence Nightingale sat down and wrote a private letter to her brother-in-law Sir Harry Verney. Verney was involved in the society sending relief to the wounded of the Franco-Prussian War, and Seacole had been asking to be sent.

Nightingale wrote that Seacole had kept, and she would not call it a bad house, but something not very unlike it. In the English of 1870 that phrase meant a brothel.

She added that Seacole had been very kind to the men and to the officers and had done some good, and had also made many of them drunk. Anybody who employed her, the letter said, would be getting the kindness and the improper conduct together.

Seacole never saw that letter, which sat in a family archive for the better part of a century.

Seacole was not friendless in those last years. Prince Victor of Hohenlohe-Langenburg, a nephew of Queen Victoria, had been a young lieutenant at Spring Hill who called her mami because he had grown up hearing Creole children use it, and in 1871 he sculpted her bust and showed it at the Royal Academy.

She was close to Princess Alexandra, and she had converted to Roman Catholicism, and she owned two houses back in Kingston. She died at her home in Paddington on the fourteenth of May 1881.

Probate was granted on the eleventh of July, and the estate came to two thousand six hundred and fifteen pounds, eleven shillings and sevenpence.

So she did not die poor, and the version that says she did is wrong. She died with money she had made herself, out of a book she had written herself, about a war her own government had refused to send her to.

Her will left a run of small legacies, a good many of them exactly nineteen guineas, and the rest to her sister Louisa. She described her late husband in it as the godson of Admiral Nelson, which is what she had always been told, and which nobody has ever been able to prove or disprove.

She was buried at St Mary's Roman Catholic Cemetery at Kensal Green, and the grave was allowed to go under. The people who came looking for it were not English.

In 1954 the nurses of Jamaica named their association headquarters in Kingston after her. That was nineteen years before anybody in England went looking for the plot.

The stone says she was a notable nurse who cared for the sick and wounded in the West Indies, in Panama, and on the battlefields of the Crimea, and it arrived a hundred and eighteen years late, paid for by nurses, most of them Caribbean women, out of their own wages.

The U.S. Coast Guard rescued 16 people after their suspected smuggling boat capsized far off the coast of Ensenada early Friday morning, but a daylong search for 11 additional victims reported to still be in the water turned up empty by nightfall.

All 16 known survivors were Mexican nationals who were taken to San Diego-area hospitals for evaluation and treatment.

As of early Friday evening, searchers had not located other survivors nor recovered the bodies of anyone who may have been aboard the doomed vessel, a Coast Guard spokesperson said. 

Someone aboard the boat put out a distress call about 1 a.m., reporting that the vessel was taking on water and that 27 people were on board, Petty Officer Charlie Valor said. Air and surface crews from across California responded, along with the U.S. Navy, and based their search area on the direction from which the radio signal had come.

A Coast Guard helicopter based out of Ventura was first to reach the site, about 2 a.m., and its crew reported finding 16 people in the water about 140 miles off Ensenada.

The rescued passengers were flown to the Coast Guard’s San Diego headquarters, where 13 ambulances were waiting to take them to hospitals for evaluation and treatment. San Diego Fire-Rescue Assistant Fire Chief Brian Raines said during an early morning news conference. 
It was not immediately clear if any had been wearing lifejackets.

The Mexican Consulate General in San Diego confirmed that the 16 known survivors were Mexican nationals. In a statement, the consulate said its staffers had visited the hospitals to offer the survivors consular assistance.

A U.S. Customs and Border Protection spokesperson confirmed that the vessel was a suspected smuggling boat.

Coast Guard officials did not provide information about the boat or the reason for its voyage. However, in a news release issued mid-morning, the Coast Guard’s San Diego sector commander alluded to human smuggling.

“This case highlights the extreme dangers of taking to the sea,” Capt. Robert Tucker said. “The vessel had a large number of people on board and was following a route normally used in illegal maritime smuggling operations".

The Coast Guard was leading Friday’s search and rescue effort, including the helicopter from Ventura, a fixed-wing plane from Sacramento and vessels based around the state, he said. The U.S. Navy was also helping.

text:
A city loaded its schoolchildren onto school buses, drove them to jail, and then threw them out of school for going. Birmingham, May 1963, and eighteen days after those buses ran the school board threw one thousand and eighty-one students out of class, having announced an Americanism curriculum two days before that.

You know the photograph with the dog. You have almost certainly never been told what the school system did once the cameras left town.

On the twentieth of May, 1963, the superintendent of Birmingham's public schools signed an order against one thousand and eighty-one Black students. The older ones lost the rest of the term outright, the younger ones were suspended, and not one of them got the hearing the board's own rules required.

His name was Theo R. Wright. Their offense was that earlier that month they had walked out of his classrooms and been arrested for marching against segregation.

The city had driven them to jail on school buses.

You know the photographs. The dogs, the water, the boy in the sweater with the officer's fist in it.

Almost nobody has been told what the school system did after the cameras packed up and went home. Start seven weeks before Wright signed anything, on the third of April, with a woman walking up the steps of Birmingham City Hall.

Lola Hendricks was thirty years old that spring, Birmingham born, Ullman and then Parker, graduated in January of 1951. She was corresponding secretary of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, and she kept Fred Shuttlesworth's calendar out of an office at Bethel Baptist Church.

Shuttlesworth had authorized her to go. Reverend Ambus Hill of Lily Grove Baptist went with her, and the two of them asked at the desk to see whoever issued permits for parading, picketing and demonstrating.

They were sent to the office of the Commissioner of Public Safety. She said her piece plainly, that they had come up to see about getting a permit for picketing, parading and demonstrating.

Eugene Connor did not need to think about it. There would be no permit in Birmingham, Alabama.

"I will picket you over to the City Jail," he told her. He said it twice, so she would not miss it.

She went back and reported the conversation word for word. Four years later the Supreme Court of the United States put her account into the record of Walker v. City of Birmingham, which is the only reason we know exactly what he said to her.

Remember her face in that office. She is going to come back into this story in a way that will knock the wind out of you.

By the end of April the campaign was dying. King had been arrested on Good Friday and had written his letter on the margins of a newspaper, and it had not filled a single jail.

The adults would not come. A night in a Birmingham cell meant a phone call to a white foreman in the morning and no job to come back to.

James Bevel started running workshops for the students instead, and he did not lecture them about justice. He asked them questions and let them answer, and the answers did the work.

Janice Wesley was sixteen, an eleventh grader at Ullman High School. She had always known what segregation was, and she said later she had never understood the size of the gap inside it.

Bevel asked about their books. They were hand-me-downs, and everybody in the room knew whose hands they had come down from.

He asked about the football helmets, and those were hand-me-downs too. He asked about typewriters, and Janice worked out that her whole school had one typewriter while the white schools across town had entire rooms of them.

She said it became personal to her. She decided she wanted to do something about it.

They were shown film of demonstrations in other cities, people being struck and spat on and dragged off lunch counter stools. Then they were told plainly that the same might happen to them, and that they could not hit back, only pray or sing.

Freeman Hrabowski was twelve, a freshman at the same school. He was sitting in the back of a church doing math problems, which is what he did with himself, when the visiting preacher said something that made him look up.

The preacher said that if children marched, America would have to face the fact that even children knew right from wrong. Freeman asked who that was, and people around him said the name twice, King, King.

His parents did not want him to go. He went.

Nine-year-old Audrey Faye Hendricks had made up her own mind before anybody asked her to. She made it up at home.

She was Lola's oldest girl, a third grader at Center Street Elementary, and the mass meetings had been the background noise of her whole childhood. When she heard the call to fill the jails she told her mother she wanted to go to jail.

Her parents thought that was a good idea. So they helped her get ready.

Her father went out and bought her a board game she had been eyeing. It was not a sentimental purchase, it was a practical one.

Sit with that a second.

A man in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963 is standing in a store picking out a toy for his nine-year-old to take to jail. He has worked out that a week is a long time on a cellblock and she is going to get bored.

On the morning of Thursday the second of May, her mother took her to school first. Not to attend, but to tell her third grade teacher why she would be absent for the rest of the week.

The teacher cried at her desk. Audrey understood that the tears were pride and not disapproval, and she remembered it that way for the rest of her life.

She went around and hugged all her grandparents goodbye, one by one, the way you do before a trip. One of her grandmothers told her she would be fine.

Then her parents drove her to the church so she could be arrested.

Wyatt Walker had already asked Lola not to march. Her work behind the scenes was worth more to the movement than her body in a cell.

So the woman who had stood in Bull Connor's office in April stayed home in May. She let her nine-year-old go in her place.

Audrey was the only child in her class who went.

Across town Janice Wesley sat through first period at Ullman with no intention of staying. She leaned over and asked a young teacher what she supposed might happen if some kids walked out of class today.

Just after noon they started coming out of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church.

Fifty at a time, two by two, singing. When one group was taken another group came out of the doors behind it, and then another.

Audrey remembered that the singing was what handled the fear. We Shall Overcome, Oh Freedom, arms locked, eight blocks of open Birmingham pavement between the church and city hall.

The police arrested them as fast as they could physically reach them, and it was not fast enough. There were not enough officers on the street and reinforcements had to be called in.

Connor ran out of paddy wagons before he ran out of children. The wagons went out full, came back, and still those church doors kept opening.

So he sent for the school buses.

This is the image nobody reproduces. It is the one I cannot stop thinking about.

Yellow school buses pulling up to the curb in downtown Birmingham. Police officers loading first graders and high school seniors up the steps of them, past the driver's seat, into the rows those same children sat in on any ordinary Tuesday.

The buses pulling away toward a jail built to hold nine hundred people. It held twelve hundred by nightfall.

Counts of that first day run from more than six hundred arrested to over nine hundred. The overflow went where it could.

Girls thirteen to eighteen were put in the 4-H Club building out at the fairgrounds. The boys went to the Jefferson County jail and the Bessemer jail, and children under thirteen were held on cellblocks with the older ones because there was nowhere else to put them.

At the county jail they were lined up to be processed like anybody else. Belongings confiscated, fingerprints taken, and then a mugshot camera going off in the face of a child who had been sitting in a third grade classroom that morning.

Janice Wesley lied about her age at the desk. Her best friend was a year younger, and she wanted to go wherever they were sending her friend.

The cells were cold. There were bunks with no mattresses on them, and a toilet in the open with no partition around it.

When the floor got too cold the girls sat on top of each other. Then they sang.

Connor gave orders that the demonstrators be questioned. Every one of them, at whatever age they happened to be.

Audrey Hendricks was nine years old.

She carried those questions the rest of her life and repeated them plainly once she was grown. Why did you march, who told you to march, did they force you to march.

Nobody had forced her. She had asked, at the kitchen table, and her mother had said yes.

Outside the fences, parents who could not get their children out stood and threw food and blankets over the wire to them. Word came back out of the buildings the same way, hand to hand through the adults inside, which is how the Hendricks family learned Audrey was alive and safe.

The next day the whole world found out.

On Friday the third of May the fire department brought monitor guns to Kelly Ingram Park. Connor bragged about the pressure on them, the kind that could strip bark off a tree from a hundred feet away.

Children went down the pavement in front of it. Bark came off the trees, bricks came loose from a wall, and a stream put Fred Shuttlesworth into the side of the church hard enough to send him to the hospital.

After the water, the dogs.

Bill Hudson of the Associated Press photographed an officer with a fistful of a teenage boy's sweater and a German shepherd at the boy's middle. The New York Times ran it the next morning three columns wide, above the fold.

Here is the thing about that picture that ought to be better known. Accounts of the young man in it disagree, and Birmingham's own historical record describes Walter Gadsden as an onlooker rather than one of the organized marchers.

So the single photograph that moved a country may not even show one of the volunteers. Of the thousands who raised their hands in that church and got on those buses, almost none are named in the image that made their sacrifice famous.

They marched again on Saturday the fourth. Every child who walked out that morning had already seen what Friday looked like.

Freeman Hrabowski was twelve and he had watched it. He led his group out of Sixth Avenue Baptist, over to Sixteenth Street, and down toward City Hall singing.

The assignment at the end of the walk was simple. Kneel on the steps of City Hall, pray for their freedom, and tell whoever was standing there what they wanted, which was school and water fountains and restaurants like anybody else.

He made it all the way to the steps. Bull Connor was standing on them.

Connor looked down at a twelve-year-old boy and asked him what he wanted, using the word he always used. Hrabowski's knees were shaking, and he said, in his Birmingham accent, that they wanted to kneel and pray.

Then they put him in a police wagon.

He was inside for five days. They held his little group with older boys jailed for real offenses, and the guards encouraged the intimidation rather than stopping it.

The job that fell to him in there was the boys from his own group. They were only a couple of years younger than he was, they cried for their mothers, and he was twelve and had nothing to give them except company.

In the middle of that week, King and the parents came and stood outside the detention center. He told the children on the other side of that wall that what they were doing would make the world better for children not yet born.

They were all crying when he said it. Hrabowski has repeated that sentence in public for sixty years.

On the tenth of May the movement and Birmingham's white business leaders announced an agreement. Fitting rooms first, then lunch counters, restrooms and drinking fountains inside ninety days, and Black clerks and salesmen hired inside sixty.

The jailed demonstrators would come out on bond. Not one line of it desegregated a single Birmingham school.

That was the whole harvest.

That night and the next, bombs went off at the Gaston Motel and at the home of King's brother. Connor denounced the agreement he had lost and suggested the city might not honor it.

The bill came due. It came for the children.

On the eighteenth of May the Board of Education announced next year's theme, and the Post-Herald printed the slogan: the development of character through the study of principles of our American way of life. Wright said he would put instruction in Americanism into every classroom.

Two days later he threw one thousand and eighty-one of them out of school for practicing it.

George Wallace called it the delinquency of minors. Wright blamed outside agitation and named one person from Cincinnati and two from Atlanta, which was how he said Shuttlesworth, King and Abernathy without having to say them.

Understand what that order meant to a family. The buses had taken your child to jail on the second of May.

On the twentieth, the school system took away the reason she had ever been on a bus in the first place. Same city, and both times it reached her through her school.

The children saw the machine more clearly than he expected.

On the twenty-first of May a crowd of the expelled and suspended gathered outside King's room at the A. G. Gaston Motel, wanting to know what happens now. He called the order a terrible, brutal, unjust and unwise act.

Then he asked them to remember who appoints the school board. The film of that meeting caught a young voice in the crowd answering: Connor.

The lawyer was Constance Baker Motley. On the morning of the twenty-second she stood in front of Judge Clarence Allgood and asked for an order stopping Wright.

Allgood refused her. He said from the bench that he had been shocked to see hundreds of school children running loose and wild over the streets of Birmingham.

Motley walked out of that courtroom and got on a plane to Atlanta the same day.

She took one named plaintiff with her, a fifth grader called Linda Cal Woods. Linda's father was a Birmingham minister, and the way Linda had gotten to the march at all was by hiding on the floor in the back of his car.

Judge Elbert Tuttle heard the case that afternoon and ruled from Atlanta. He said the students had been engaged in legally permissible activities and illegally arrested for exercising a constitutional right.

He told the board what it had actually done. It amounted to knocking out five hundred student years of study.

Then he ordered Wright to have every one of them back inside a classroom by the following morning.

Four thousand people packed St. James Church that night. The Baltimore Afro-American described a screaming, flag-waving crowd that nearly took the roof off the building.

Four months later a bomb at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church killed four girls, and one of them was named Cynthia Wesley.

Janice Wesley was not related to her. The two of them had the same last name and had decided, the way girls do, to tell everybody they were sisters.

That is the building those thousand children had walked out of in May, singing, in groups of fifty. It is the building the world remembers for September, and that is part of why the buses and the expulsion fell out of the story entirely.

So here is what those children are actually owed, and it is not outrage. King told them through a wall that what they were doing would reach children who had not been born.

You are one of the children he was talking about. So is every Black child who has walked into a school, a store, a courtroom or a job in this country since.

That bill was paid in full. It was paid by a nine-year-old with a board game, a twelve-year-old sitting up with sobbing eight-year-olds, and a fifth grader lying on the floorboard of her father's car.

Carry their names out of here. Audrey Hendricks, Freeman Hrabowski, Janice Wesley, Linda Cal Woods.

The photograph never did.

On the eleventh of August, 2009, the mayor of Birmingham offered a blanket pardon to some two thousand five hundred people the city had arrested during the movement. Forty-six years late, and most of them did not want it.

Audrey Faye Hendricks was never offered it. She was already gone.

She had gone to college, taught school in Dallas, then come home to Birmingham and spent twenty-five years working with poor children there. She died on the first of March that year.

One of the women who turned the pardon down was Gwendolyn Webb-Happling, who was fourteen in 1963 and did her week out at the fairgrounds. She had a reason, and she said it out loud in front of reporters.

"We went to jail for a purpose, to be free."

text:
I've had the pleasure of reading @JibrielBraithw2's thread about competitive yugioh content and I wanted to share my opinion, even if I'm really no one to change the overall discussion obv.

I do think that the points that Jib wants to highlight are overall correct and do need a bit of a discussion. 

First of all, let's address the negativity aspect in the community. 
I've heard an insane amount of people just say the following sentence "Yugioh advanced is unplayable" and honestly hearing this just infuriates me. 
This is because these sentences usually come from people that are not actively competing / trying to do something meaningful when they play the game, so it's just a random opinion copied from some negative thread/video seen online: Nothing is personal, nothing comes really from the person saying these things. It's all a copy pasta and this is insane to me, how is this possible???

Having said this, I am not unaware that the game was in an undesirable spot before the banlist (even after the 34 card E-banlist some issues are still there, because Konami had to make some people with bad/non-competitive takes happy), but I do also think that every good "pro-player" showed us that they can perform even if the format is "bad". They simply performed over and over again. This is no coincidence and no luck!
I've had the pleasure to exchange opinions (both for the game and for my YT start, still thanks for the advices 🩷) with @TrifGaming before YCS Houston and trust me that if this guy does this well so consistently is because he puts in the work, nothing more and nothing less! He wasn't wasting time complaining that X card was still legal, he just found a way to make the format playable for himself!

Second of all I wanted to say something that is more close to my personal situation: the lack of good yugioh content online.
I know that I'm still a very small channel, but I'm really trying my best to provide a good and valid content online, that can compare to what paid content can offer, to help out people that can't afford to pay 40/50 dollars every month or so in order to purchase metafy content. 

The reason behind opening my channel is because I felt myself that YouTube had very few good content creators making competitive Yugioh videos. I immediately tried putting in all of my testing in order to give everyone watching my video as much help as possible, even if my income was and still is ZERO. I learnt how to edit (thanks Jake <3), how to setup OBS (still thanks @Hypnocorn), how to make thumbnails (ok that's kind of a lie, they're kidna troll, I stole the idea from Santoli's), how to adjust YT setting for videos and I also bought better hardware, like a new mic, just for the love of this game and its community!

I also want to say that I'm the first one who makes Metafy content, I do that since 2025, way before I started making youtube content.
The reason behind my decision to just release content for FREE (Yeah, I make the grand amount of ZERO cents on YT) is because I wanted to give something in return to this game and its community in one of the worst historical moments of the game: a moment where everyone dooms and glooms because "x person said so".
The only thing that I do in order to "promote" my paid content is to take 10 seconds of the video to remember it exists and put it in the description, but that's it! The other 35+ minutes of EVERY VIDEO are there, free to see for everyone and full of content that comes out straight from the sum of my testing, which are multiple hours condensed in some minutes for you and for free.

Having said that, sorry for the long message, but I felt like I had to say something in this regard. 
The only thing I can want to say after writing this is that I am really glad that I've had so much insane support from all my friends, sharing my content and pushing me insanely hard for this new beginning. I can't tag all of them because the list would be infinite, but yeah still I can't express my gratitude enough. 

I really enjoy playing yugioh and I will continue doing as much as possible for the community, being free, paid or whichever form of content that can help out whoever needs, that's the only thing that matters at the end of the day.

⚖️ James Comey has been charged a third time. Prosecutors accuse the ex-FBI director of violating the Espionage Act by leaking classified information to a reporter in 2016.
The two counts, transmitting national defense information and conspiring to do it, were filed under seal Oct. 5 and unsealed Monday by U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden at Comey's request. What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

Civil Twilight:  
Begins in the morning, or ends in the evening, when the geometric center of the SUN is 6 degrees below the horizon.  Therefore morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, and ends at sunrise.  Evening civil twilight begins at sunset, and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon.  Under these conditions absent fog or other restrictions, the brightest stars and planets can be seen, the horizon and terrestrial objects can be discerned, and in many cases, artificial lighting is not needed. Civil Twilight is also known as Civil Dawn and Civil Dusk.
Nautical Twilight:
Begins in the morning, or ends in the evening, when the geometric center of the sun is 12 degrees below the horizon.  In general, the term nautical twilight refers to sailors being able to take reliable readings via well known stars because the horizon is still visible, even under moonless conditions.  Absent fog or other restrictions, outlines of terrestrial objects may still be discernible, but detailed outdoor activities are likely curtailed without artificial illumination. Nautical Twilight is also known as Nautical Dawn and Nautical Dusk.
Astronomical Twilight:
Begins in the morning, or ends in the evening, when the geometric center of the sun is 18 degrees below the horizon.  In astronomical twilight, sky illumination is so faint that most casual observers would regard the sky as fully dark, especially under urban or suburban light pollution.  Under astronomical twilight, the horizon is not discernible and moderately faint stars or planets can be observed with the naked eye under a non light polluted sky.  But to test the limits of naked eye observations, the sun needs to be more than 18 degrees below the horizon.  Point light sources such as stars and planets can be readily studied by astronomers under astronomical twilight.  But diffuse light sources such as galaxies, nebula, and globular clusters need to be observed under a totally dark sky, again when the sun is more than 18 degrees below the horizon.

My friends @patrickqmason (Holds the Leonard J. Arrington Chair of Mormon History and Culture at Utah State University) and Melissa Mason  (Clinical Social Worker, Master of Social Work, Utah State University) join us to talk about their new book called “Rooted:  Centering Christ in Everything”

The authors share that too often, Latter-day Saints have centered their religious lives on rules, worthiness, obedience, institutional loyalty, and cultural expectations rather than on Jesus Christ Himself.  They invite readers to rethink what it means to be a disciple of Christ—placing greater emphasis on grace, compassion, love, belonging, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ.

Their message isn't that commandments, covenants, or Church participation don't matter. Rather, these things should point us toward Christ, not become substitutes for Him.  They offer practical suggestions to bring Christ the focus of our church talks, lessons, conversation—and in all aspects of our lives.

This is a super powerful podcast to help all of us better focus on Christ.  Thank you, Melissa and Patick, for being on the podcast.  I encourage everyone to read their book as we work to become a more Zion people.
